chapters.title: Chapter 5: Putting Your Tax Plan Into Action

lessons.title: Case Study: Three Indian Taxpayers Build Their 80C Plan

children.text: This course has covered every piece of Section 80C on its own. Now we put it together, the way you will in real life. Three taxpayers, three very different situations, one process: check the regime, count what already qualifies, match the gap to goals, and choose on merit. Their conclusions are different, and one of them decides not to use 80C at all. That is the point.

cells: Rents in Mumbai, MBA education loan, EPF ₹90,000
₹30 lakh in a new SCSS account, FDs, health cover for both

children.text: Case 1: Riya, the First-Jobber Who Skips 80C

Riya's colleagues are buying ELSS in March and her father wants her to start an LIC policy. Before doing anything, she runs step one: compare the regimes, assuming she maxes out 80C and claims ₹25,000 under Section 126 (80D) for her own health cover on the old regime.

body.label: Riya's verdict
body.context: Even a perfect old-regime plan would cost her ₹91,000 in tax and require ₹1,06,800 of extra 80C investments. The new regime gets her to zero with complete freedom over how she invests.

body.title: Riya's Next Move
body.question: Riya is on the new regime with zero tax. She has ₹1,20,000 a year to save beyond EPF and wants to retire comfortably. What is the most sensible approach?
options: Buy an endowment policy anyway, since it is 'safe'
Invest in ELSS to use up her 80C limit
Build an emergency fund first, then invest for long-term goals in low-cost equity index funds, with PPF optional for tax-free stability
Keep everything in a savings account until she switches to the old regime
body.explanation: With no tax benefit from 80C, Riya should choose purely on merit. An emergency fund comes first. For long-term growth, a regular index fund gives equity exposure without ELSS's 3-year lock-in. PPF still earns 7.1% tax-free on the new regime, so it is a reasonable choice for the stable portion even without the deduction. An endowment policy makes little sense with no dependents.

children.text: Case 2: Meera, Where the Old Regime Wins

Meera's basic salary is ₹7,50,000 a year. She receives ₹3,75,000 as HRA and pays ₹35,000 a month in rent in Mumbai. She is repaying an MBA loan with ₹80,000 of interest this year, and pays health insurance premiums for herself and her senior citizen parents. Her EPF of ₹90,000 leaves a ₹60,000 gap in her 80C limit.

body.title: How Meera's HRA exemption is worked out

content.caption: HRA exemption is the lowest of three amounts

cells: 50% of basic, since Mumbai is a metro city

content.text: Her landlord's PAN is required because yearly rent exceeds ₹1 lakh, and Form 124 now asks her to disclose her relationship with the landlord.

body.caption: Meera's tax under both regimes, with her full plan

body.title: Meera's ₹7,50,000 of old-regime exemptions and deductions

children.text: The old regime saves Meera ₹18,200. But look at how thin that margin is. It depends on her actually investing the ₹60,000 in ELSS and ₹50,000 in NPS. Her ELSS goes into a monthly SIP for retirement, since she is 34 and ticked every box on the risk check. The NPS contribution suits the same goal.

body.title: Your Turn: What If She Skips ELSS?
body.prompt: Suppose Meera does everything else in her plan but never invests the ₹60,000 in ELSS, so her 80C claim is only her EPF of ₹90,000. What would her old-regime tax be, including 4% cess?
body.explanation: Her taxable income rises by ₹60,000, from ₹10,50,000 to ₹11,10,000. Tax = ₹12,500 + ₹1,00,000 + 30% of ₹1,10,000 (₹33,000) = ₹1,45,500, plus 4% cess = ₹1,51,320. That is ₹520 more than her new-regime tax of ₹1,50,800, so skipping the ELSS would make the new regime the cheaper choice.

body.text: The lesson from Meera's case: the old regime only wins if you actually make the investments you plan. If her ELSS and NPS contributions fall through, the new regime becomes cheaper. Check the comparison again in December, before the proof deadline, and choose your final regime when you file.

children.text: Case 3: Joseph, Where SCSS Is About Income, Not Tax

Joseph retired as a branch manager at a public sector bank. His first SCSS account matured this year and he reinvested ₹30,00,000 into a fresh account at 8.2%, which pays ₹61,500 a quarter. His income: pension ₹6,00,000, SCSS interest ₹2,46,000, FD interest ₹60,000 and savings interest ₹12,000, for a total of ₹9,18,000. He and his wife pay ₹55,000 for health insurance. His friends tell him the SCSS deposit 'saves ₹1.5 lakh of tax'.

body.label: Joseph's verdict
body.context: SCSS is still the right home for his ₹30 lakh: government-backed, fixed at 8.2% for 5 years, with quarterly income. It just is not saving him any tax.

body.title: Joseph's TDS Problem
body.textWithBlank: Joseph's SCSS interest exceeds ₹1 lakh, so 10% TDS will be deducted even though his final tax is zero. To avoid this, he can submit Form ___ to the post office or bank.
body.explanation: From 1 April 2026, Form 121 replaces Forms 15G and 15H. Since the tax on his estimated total income for the year is nil under the new regime, he can submit it at the start of the year. Otherwise he would have ₹24,600 deducted on SCSS interest alone and have to wait for a refund.

body.text: Section 80C is a tool, not a ritual. Use it when the numbers say so, and invest on merit when they do not.

body.title: Your Own Case
body.scenario: You now have everything you need to build your own plan: the regime comparison, the full list of 80C options, the post-tax comparison, the goal and risk filters, and the paperwork process.
body.prompt: Write down your own case in the same format as Riya, Meera and Joseph: income, what already qualifies under 80C, other deductions, goals and risk profile. Then answer: which regime wins, what is your real 80C gap, and what will you put it into?
body.modelAnswer: A strong answer follows the same five steps used in the case studies. (1) Regime: calculate tax under both regimes using your realistic deductions, not your hopeful ones. If the new regime wins, stop here and invest on merit. (2) Count what qualifies automatically: EPF, tuition fees, home loan principal, existing life premiums. (3) Find the gap: ₹1,50,000 minus that total, and consider Section 124(3) NPS for another ₹50,000 if you are on the old regime. (4) Match the gap to goals and horizons: nothing under 3 years, NSC or 5-year deposits for 3 to 5 years, PPF, ELSS, NPS or SSY for 10 years and beyond. (5) Filter by risk and choose the best post-tax option, then set it up as an April SIP or standing instruction and put the proof submission dates in your calendar. Revisit the comparison each year, because salary, rent, loans and family circumstances change which regime wins.

body.title: Your 80C Action Plan
steps: Calculate your tax under both regimes with realistic deductions
List every automatic 80C item and find your real gap
Assign the gap to goals with clear time horizons
Run the risk check and choose the best post-tax option for each goal
Set up SIPs or standing instructions in April, with PPF deposits before the 5th
Declare your regime and Form 124 figures to HR
Recheck the regime comparison in December and submit proofs on time
File by 31 July, claiming everything you are entitled to

points: Always compare both regimes first; for many salaried taxpayers and retirees with income up to about ₹12 lakh, the new regime wins without any 80C.
The old regime tends to win when large exemptions and deductions stack up: HRA, education loan interest, parents' health insurance, NPS and a full 80C.
When the old regime wins narrowly, it only wins if you actually make the planned investments.
Products like SCSS and PPF can still be the right choice on the new regime, for safety and income rather than tax.
Manage TDS with Form 124 declarations and, where your tax is nil, Form 121.
Revisit your plan every year, because the right regime and the right 80C mix change as your life changes.

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and is not tax, legal or investment advice. The case studies are illustrative, use simplified assumptions (no surcharge, no other income, standard HRA rules) and reflect slab rates for tax year 2026-27. Consult a qualified Chartered Accountant or SEBI-registered investment adviser for decisions specific to your situation.
